glossary.definition: A camera transfer encoding that preserves more tonal information in shadows, midtones and highlights than display-referred Rec.709; log footage looks flat and desaturated and serves as a grading canvas, not a deliverable [FACT/excerpt - log/Rec.709 explainers, grounding sources 23-24].

The standard SDR delivery color space for display-referred video; the target this pipeline grades INTO and delivers to Instagram in [FACT/excerpt - sources 23-24]. AI video models are assumed to already deliver Rec.709-ish display-referred files [ESTIMATE - typical of consumer AI video delivery; exact Higgsfield specs UNKNOWN, MCP-surface file].

A stored transform mapping input color values to output values, with two distinct roles: technical LUTs (e.g., log-to-Rec.709 normalization, applied FIRST) and creative LUTs (looks, applied LAST, intensity-controllable) [FACT/excerpt - sources 23-24]. A LUT is a dumb transform: applied to unbalanced clips it amplifies mismatch [ESTIMATE - colorist craft, high confidence].

The dominant 2000s+ blockbuster grade: orange and teal are complements with maximal exposure-value contrast among complementary pairs; skin sits in the orange range, so pushing shadows/backgrounds teal makes subjects pop, partly replicating golden hour (warm light vs blue sky) [FACT/excerpt - Adobe/PetaPixel explainers, sources 25-26].

The one clip per reel declared as the match reference — chosen for best skin rendering plus best exposure — that every other clip is matched TO on the scopes before the house creative LUT goes on top [FACT/excerpt on the base Resolve shot-matching method - source 28; per-reel adaptation ESTIMATE, high confidence].

The fixed hue line on the vectorscope along which human skin hue clusters regardless of complexion depth; colorists refine skin on the vectorscope after balancing luminance on the waveform and white balance on the RGB parade [FACT/excerpt - Resolve shot-matching guide, source 28].

A small stored correction (offset/temperature/saturation nudge toward the house target) maintained per AI video model and applied before hero matching, learned from a model's first batches because different models are expected to carry systematic color signatures [ESTIMATE - process design; actual signatures UNKNOWN until generation runs].

An AI-specific intra-clip failure mode classic footage lacks: colors and details wandering WITHIN one clip (plus flicker); cited mitigations are short 3-5 s segments, simple consistent lighting prompts ('3-5 lighting adjectives'), and a master reference image via image-to-video [FACT/excerpt - AI-video consistency guides, sources 29-31; vendor/practitioner guides, not peer-reviewed].

Visible stepping in smooth gradients (skies, luxury-interior walls, vignettes) because 8-bit gives only 256 levels per channel; social delivery is 8-bit 4:2:0, so banding risk is structural; countered by high-bit-depth grading, fine dither/grain ~1-2%, and deband filtering [FACT/excerpt - banding/debanding guides, sources 33-34].

Shadow detail lost at or near code value 0; heavy encoders crush near-black macroblocks first, so intentional shadow detail is kept a few code values above 0 and verified on a phone after an actual test upload, not just in the NLE [ESTIMATE - colorist craft plus codec behavior, medium-high confidence per the grounding file].

nodes.definition: Fix the two color-space concepts the whole grading chain reasons between. Log encodings preserve more tonal information in shadows, midtones and highlights than display-referred Rec.709; log footage looks flat and desaturated and is a grading CANVAS, while Rec.709 is the standard SDR DELIVERY color space [FACT/excerpt - log/Rec.709 explainers, sources 23-24]. The distinction matters even in an AI pipeline that may never touch true log, because it defines what 'normalization' means (get to an accurate display-referred image before creative decisions) and why the delivery target for Instagram is Rec.709/SDR. An expert who conflates canvas and delivery either grades on an unconverted flat image (every decision miscalibrated) or ships a flat log-ish file to a platform expecting Rec.709.

nodes.definition: Ground every match and skin decision in scopes, not perception. The professional shot-matching practice reads three instruments in a fixed question order: luminance levels on the WAVEFORM, white balance on the RGB PARADE, and skin hue on the VECTORSCOPE, where skin tones cluster along the skin-tone indicator line; colorists refine skin on the vectorscope only after luminance and white balance are set [FACT/excerpt - Resolve shot-matching guide, source 28]. Scopes matter doubly for AI footage: per-clip drift is subtle enough that adapted eyes normalize it, and the mobile-editing reality means scope-based matching needs a desktop grader (Resolve's free tier includes scopes, groups and shot-match), pushing the pipeline toward hybrid mobile-assemble / desktop-grade [ESTIMATE - tooling landscape, medium confidence per grounding file].

the skin-tone indicator line
why scope-based matching implies a desktop grading stage
excluded: the full hero-match procedure that uses this order (HERO_MATCH_PROCEDURE)
mobile assembly and beat-marking (editing-craft KB)

pros.claim: Scopes give an objective reference that defeats eye adaptation across dozens of subtly mismatched AI clips
pros.example: the parade revealing a warm cast on a clip the adapted eye had already accepted as neutral after ten minutes of grading

cons.claim: Scope discipline forces a desktop tool into an otherwise mobile-friendly reel pipeline, adding a workflow hop
cons.example: round-tripping clips from a phone assembly into Resolve and back solely to get waveform/parade/vectorscope reads

failure_modes: matching clips by eye only and shipping a reel whose casts reappear on other screens

base.update_signal: new tooling with mobile scopes or an eye-vs-scope mismatch incident changes the discipline

nodes.definition: Enforce the industry-standard grading chain order: (1) technical normalization FIRST — a log-to-Rec.709 conversion LUT or color-space transform so decisions are made on an accurate image; (2) primary corrections (exposure, white balance, contrast); (3) secondaries (skin isolation, masks/windows); (4) the creative look/LUT LAST in the chain [FACT/excerpt - grading workflow guides, sources 23-24]. The order is not stylistic preference but error containment: every stage assumes the previous stage delivered a trustworthy image, so a look applied before balancing bakes per-clip errors into the style, and a secondary keyed on an unbalanced image keys the wrong pixels. In this KB every downstream node (hero matching, LUT baking, skin protection) is a specialization of one slot in this chain.

excluded: what normalization concretely means for AI clips (AI_DELIVERY_NORMALIZATION)

pros.claim: A fixed chain order contains errors stage by stage so a bad look never contaminates the correction underneath it
pros.example: dialing the house LUT's intensity down without touching the per-clip balance because the balance lives upstream of the look

cons.claim: Strict staging adds ceremony that feels heavy for a 15-second reel of five clips
cons.example: building normalization, primary and secondary stages per clip when a one-click filter would 'look fine' on a single phone screen

nodes.definition: Understand WHY teal-orange works before deciding how much of it to use. Orange and teal are complements with maximal exposure-value contrast among complementary pairs; skin tones sit in the orange range, so pushing shadows and backgrounds toward teal makes human subjects pop from the frame; the look dominates 2000s+ blockbusters and partly replicates golden hour (warm light against blue sky) [FACT/excerpt - Adobe/PetaPixel explainers, sources 25-26]. The mechanism — hue-complement separation anchored on skin — is what the luxury variant keeps; the blockbuster INTENSITY is what it discards. Grading decisions that skip the mechanism and copy the intensity produce the loud, gauche version the classic-luxurious brief explicitly avoids.

skin in the orange range as the separation anchor
the golden-hour replication reading
excluded: the restrained luxury dosage of the effect (WARM_NEUTRAL_LUXURY_LOOK)

pros.claim: Knowing the mechanism lets separation be dosed — a whisper of teal still separates because the complement relation, not the saturation, does the work
pros.example: achieving subject pop on a beige-marble interior with a barely-visible cool shadow drift instead of a saturated teal wall

nodes.definition: Design the house look as the warm-neutral filmic / 'old money' variant, NOT full blockbuster teal-orange. Palette basis: warm, muted, timeless — cream, beige, camel, navy, sage, taupe, tobacco; nothing neon; warm practical light (~2700-3000 K look) reads richer than cool light [FACT/excerpt - old-money-aesthetic style guides, source 27; the palette-to-grade mapping is ESTIMATE]. Grade translation [ESTIMATE - colorist craft, medium-high confidence]: keep skin warm-natural; drift shadows only slightly cool (a whisper of teal, not a wall); desaturate global chroma ~10-20% below default; ROLL OFF highlights rather than letting whites clip — muted highlights are the strongest single 'expensive film' cue; gentle S-curve with lifted-but-not-milky blacks. This one look, baked later as the house LUT, is what covers, reels and both personas all share.

nodes.definition: Protect skin as the non-negotiable realism anchor. Skin tones are the reference the audience calibrates 'real' against; in vectorscope terms skin hue clusters along the skin-tone indicator line, refined after luminance (waveform) and white balance (parade) are set [FACT/excerpt - source 28]. Both personas' skin must land on the SAME target values across every clip and every post: skin consistency IS character consistency at the grade layer.

nodes.definition: Bake and place the house LUT correctly. A LUT is a stored transform mapping input color values to output values, in two roles: technical LUTs (log-to-Rec.709 normalization, applied first) and creative LUTs (looks, applied last, intensity-controllable) [FACT/excerpt - sources 23-24]. One baked look is also the mechanism that makes reels, covers and the fitness trim share a single source of truth for the brand grade.

nodes.definition: Declare ONE hero clip per reel as the match target before any matching starts, chosen for best skin rendering plus best exposure [FACT/excerpt on the reference-clip shot-matching method - source 28; per-reel adaptation ESTIMATE, high confidence]. The hero is the concrete answer to 'match to WHAT?' — without it, clips get matched pairwise and errors chain across the timeline. Selection discipline: the hero must itself pass the exposure gate (skin at correct level on the waveform, highlights rolled not clipped, blacks not crushed), because a clipped or crushed hero makes every other clip inherit an irrecoverable flaw; a candidate with the best skin but clipped highlights is disqualified. The hero's balanced state, before the house LUT, is the reference every per-clip normalization aims at.

included: one hero per reel chosen on best skin plus best exposure
the hero's own exposure gate (no clip/crush)
the hero as the target of all per-clip normalization
excluded: the scope-order matching mechanics (HERO_MATCH_PROCEDURE)
regeneration decisions for failed candidates (director-loop rubric, other KB)

pros.claim: A single declared reference prevents pairwise matching where small errors chain across the timeline
pros.example: five clips each matched to the hero staying within one window, versus clip 5 matched through clips 4, 3, 2 accumulating three rounds of drift

cons.claim: The whole reel inherits the hero's rendering biases, so a subtly flawed hero systematically skews every clip
cons.example: a hero with slightly magenta-biased skin pulling all four other clips magenta during matching

failure_modes: matching clips to each other instead of to one declared hero
declaring a hero with clipped highlights or crushed blacks and propagating an irrecoverable flaw
acceptance_tests: the analysis declares exactly one hero per reel on best-skin-plus-best-exposure and shows the hero passing the no-clip/no-crush exposure gate before matching begins
revisit_triggers: a better candidate clip arrives after regeneration
the declared hero is later found flawed on scopes and the reel needs re-matching

base.update_signal: a superior candidate or a discovered hero flaw forces re-declaration and re-match

nodes.definition: Match every other clip to the hero in the professional scope order: luminance on the WAVEFORM first, then white balance on the RGB PARADE, then skin on the VECTORSCOPE; automated 'shot match to this clip' is a starting point only — always refine by eye plus scopes [FACT/excerpt on the base Resolve method - source 28; adaptation to AI reels ESTIMATE, high confidence]. This is the operational core of the KB's real problem: clips from different generation batches and different models arrive with slightly different color temperature, contrast and saturation even when content is consistent, and a unified color grade applied in post is cited as 'the single most effective way to make disparate clips feel like they belong to the same video' [FACT/excerpt - AI-video consistency guides, sources 29-30]. The match happens at the balance layer, under the house LUT, never by bending the LUT per clip.

included: the waveform-then-parade-then-vectorscope match order
auto shot-match as a start only, refined by eye plus scopes
matching at the balance layer under the LUT
excluded: hero selection (HERO_CLIP_DECLARATION)
per-model pre-corrections applied before this step (PER_MODEL_TRIM_PRESETS)

pros.claim: The fixed scope order resolves the three mismatch dimensions in dependency order so later fixes do not undo earlier ones
pros.example: setting luminance before white balance so the parade read is not skewed by an exposure gap, then touching skin last

cons.claim: Per-clip scope matching is the pipeline's largest manual time cost and grows linearly with clip count
cons.example: a 9-clip 30-second reel needing eight full waveform/parade/vectorscope passes even when auto-match lands close

failure_modes: trusting automated shot-match output without scope refinement
matching in the wrong order and chasing interacting corrections
bending the house LUT per clip instead of correcting under it
acceptance_tests: the analysis matches each clip to the hero in waveform-then-parade-then-vectorscope order, treats auto-match as a starting point only, and performs corrections under (not inside) the house LUT
revisit_triggers: auto-match quality improves enough to change the manual refinement budget
a cut-boundary QC failure traces back to a matching miss
per-model presets change what the matcher receives

base.update_signal: better auto-match tooling or recurring QC failures change the match procedure

nodes.definition: Group clips per scene or per location so shared corrections propagate instead of being re-entered clip by clip [FACT/excerpt - grouping step of the Resolve shot-matching procedure, source 28]. In this pipeline groups map naturally to the reel's locations (villa interior, seafront, gym) and to generation batches: clips generated from the same master reference and lighting prompt share most of their cast, so one group-level correction plus small per-clip trims replaces N full corrections. Groups also localize rework — when the house look or a location's balance changes, the change lands once at group level, and when a QC failure implicates a whole location, the group is the natural re-grade unit [ESTIMATE - direct operationalization, high confidence].

groups mapped to locations and generation batches
groups as the rework-localization unit
excluded: which locations the reel contains (director/cinematography files)
the group feature mechanics of any specific NLE version

pros.claim: Group-level corrections turn N per-clip fixes into one shared fix plus small trims
pros.example: warming the entire seafront group once when the location reads too cool instead of editing six clips separately

cons.claim: Wrong group membership silently applies a location's correction to a clip that does not share its cast
cons.example: a golden-hour balcony clip dropped into the midday-interior group and inheriting an inappropriate warm offset

failure_modes: skipping grouping and re-entering identical corrections per clip
grouping by timeline order instead of by scene/location/batch so corrections misapply
acceptance_tests: the analysis groups clips by scene/location (or generation batch) and demonstrates one shared correction propagating with only small per-clip trims remaining
revisit_triggers: a reel structure with new locations changes the grouping scheme

base.update_signal: new locations or a group-misapplication incident changes the grouping scheme

nodes.definition: Handle cross-MODEL drift with learned trim presets. Higgsfield exposes multiple video models, and systematic per-model color signatures are EXPECTED — but the actual signatures are [UNKNOWN until generation runs]; the honest process is to LEARN a small per-model trim preset (offset/temperature/saturation nudge toward the house target) from each model's first batches, then apply it BEFORE the hero-match step so the manual match starts from a smaller gap [ESTIMATE - process design grounded in the per-model-signature observation, medium confidence per grounding file]. The preset is a prior, not an authority: the hero match remains the final arbiter per clip, and a preset that no longer helps (model version update, new signature) must be relearned rather than trusted. No signature value may ever be asserted from memory — only measured from real batches.

the learn-from-first-batches trim preset applied before hero matching
the preset-as-prior, hero-match-as-authority rule
excluded: which models exist and their parameters (MCP-surface file)
asserting any concrete signature before it is measured

pros.example: measuring that one model's clips consistently arrive warmer and more saturated, saving that nudge, and having later batches land near the hero before hand-matching

cons.claim: Presets learned from small first batches can encode batch noise as if it were the model's signature
cons.example: a trim learned from three sunset clips of one model wrongly cooling that model's daylight clips ever after

failure_modes: inventing a per-model signature from memory instead of measuring it
letting a stale preset survive a model version update
treating the preset as final instead of pre-correction before hero matching
acceptance_tests: the analysis carries the [UNKNOWN until generation runs] tag on actual signatures, derives each trim only from measured first batches, applies it before the hero match, and keeps the hero match as the final authority

nodes.definition: Handle the intra-clip failure modes classic footage does not have: TEMPORAL DRIFT (colors/details wandering within a clip) and FLICKER. Cited mitigations: generate short 3-5 s segments (already the owner's format), keep lighting prompts simple and consistent — '3-5 lighting adjectives', e.g. 'soft, diffused, consistent morning light' is more stable than a complex description — and use a master reference image via image-to-video to anchor light direction and specularity [FACT/excerpt - AI-video consistency guides, sources 29-31; these are vendor/practitioner guides, not peer-reviewed]. Grade-side triage [ESTIMATE - high confidence]: a clip that matches the hero at frame 1 but drifts mid-clip cannot be fixed by a static correction; options in cost order are trim to the stable segment, regenerate, and only last a keyframed correction, which fights the drift frame by frame and often loses.

included: temporal drift and flicker as AI-specific intra-clip failures
the three cited mitigations with their practitioner-guide caveat
grade-side triage order trim, regenerate, keyframe-last
excluded: writing the lighting prompts themselves (prompting file)
morph/artifact taxonomy beyond color (prompting/QC file)

pros.claim: Recognizing drift as intra-clip stops wasted effort on static corrections that can only be right for one frame
pros.example: trimming a 5 s clip to its stable middle 3.5 s instead of iterating a global grade that matches the head and misses the tail

cons.claim: The mitigations come from vendor/practitioner guides, not peer-reviewed sources, so their reliability across models is unverified
cons.example: the 3-5-lighting-adjectives heuristic helping on one model and doing nothing measurable on another

failure_modes: applying a static correction to a drifting clip and shipping a mid-clip color shift
burning credits on keyframed rescue when a trim or regeneration is cheaper
acceptance_tests: the analysis names drift and flicker as intra-clip AI failures, cites the three mitigations with the practitioner-guide caveat, and orders remedies trim, regenerate, keyframe-last
revisit_triggers: real generation runs show which mitigations actually reduce drift per model

base.update_signal: per-model drift behavior measured on real runs replaces the practitioner-guide priors

nodes.definition: Run the final matching QC at the cuts, where mismatch is actually seen. Step through EVERY cut boundary in the reel: the two frames either side of each cut must sit within a tight luminance/hue window; this check doubles as the transition-side requirement that luminance and hue at the two boundary frames match closely so the cut reads as intentional [FACT/excerpt on the QC step and the boundary-match requirement - sources 28 and 18-19 via the grounding file's shot-matching procedure and transition checklist]. The boundary window is the pipeline's contract with the editing-craft KB: whips, match cuts and invisible cuts all assume the grade layer delivered matched boundary frames. A reel passes grading only when every boundary passes; a failed boundary sends the offending clip back to hero matching, not to a one-off boundary hack.

the QC pass as the grade layer's contract with transition execution
failed boundaries routing back to hero matching
excluded: executing the transitions themselves (editing-craft KB)
the frame-pair design that pre-empts this check (REFERENCE_FRAME_PAIR_GRADING)

pros.claim: Checking at cut boundaries tests exactly the frames viewers compare, catching mismatch that whole-clip averages hide
pros.example: two clips whose average grades match on scopes but whose adjoining frames differ because one ends on a bright doorway, caught only at the boundary

cons.claim: A boundary-only pass can miss mid-clip drift that never touches a cut frame
cons.example: a clip drifting warm in its middle second while both its boundary frames sit inside the window

failure_modes: QCing whole-clip averages instead of the two frames at each cut
patching a failed boundary with a local hack instead of re-matching the clip
skipping boundaries on 'obviously fine' hard cuts
acceptance_tests: the analysis steps through every cut boundary, holds both adjacent frames to a tight luminance/hue window, and routes failures back to hero matching rather than boundary-local patches
revisit_triggers: the editing-craft KB changes its transition inventory and boundary expectations

base.update_signal: a visible shipped mismatch or a transition-inventory change retightens the boundary window

nodes.definition: Push boundary matching upstream to the still stage. The pipeline plans each reel as a chain of stills where clip i's END image and clip i+1's START image are designed as a PAIR; the grade layer's rule for all pairs: same house grade target, same skin values, luminance of the two frames within a narrow window — pairs failing on either frame are regenerated BEFORE video generation, which is the cheap place to fail [ESTIMATE - operationalization per grounding file, medium-high confidence; the cost ordering that stills are cheaper than video on credit-based platforms is FACT as a category, exact Higgsfield credit prices UNKNOWN here]. Constraint carried from the research: end-frame conditioning controls the BOUNDARY, not the path — mid-clip motion can still wander, so a graded matching pair does not exempt the clip from drift triage and cut-boundary QC [FACT/excerpt on short-segment stability - source 29].

included: grade/skin/luminance requirements on designed start-end frame pairs
regenerate-at-the-still-stage as the cheap failure point
the boundary-not-path constraint of end-frame conditioning
excluded: which models expose start/end-frame conditioning (MCP-surface file, UNKNOWN here)
transition-type frame pairing rules beyond color (editing-craft KB)

pros.claim: Grading the frame pairs before generation converts expensive video-stage failures into cheap still-stage rejections
pros.example: rejecting a start image whose luminance sits far from its paired end image and regenerating the still, instead of discovering the mismatch after spending video credits

cons.claim: Matched boundary stills guarantee nothing about the generated middle, so the check can create false confidence
cons.example: a perfectly paired doorway transition whose generated clip drifts teal for a second in the middle and still needs triage

acceptance_tests: the analysis applies same-grade-target, same-skin-values and the luminance window to every start/end pair, regenerates failing stills before video generation, and states the boundary-not-path constraint
revisit_triggers: the MCP-surface file confirms which models expose start/end-frame conditioning

nodes.definition: Defend gradients against banding before Instagram's re-encode. Mechanics: 8-bit gives 256 levels per channel, insufficient for smooth gradients (skies, luxury-interior walls, vignettes); social delivery is 8-bit 4:2:0, so banding risk is STRUCTURAL, and Instagram re-encoding already-compressed sources produces blockiness and banding [FACT/excerpt - banding/bit-depth guides and compression-fix guides, sources 32-34]. Countermeasures with citable basis: grade and render in higher bit depth as long as possible; add fine dither/film grain (~1-2%) to break up smooth areas; use a deband filter (e.g., Resolve's Deband) on affected regions [FACT/excerpt - sources 33-34]. The luxury look raises the stakes: its smooth beige walls, soft vignettes and rolled highlights are exactly the low-detail gradients banding attacks first.

included: the 8-bit/256-level and 4:2:0 structural-risk mechanics
high-bit-depth grading, ~1-2% dither/grain, deband filtering
why the luxury look's smooth surfaces are extra exposed
excluded: encode bitrates and upload settings (DELIVERY_ENCODE_SETTINGS)
grain's brand/anti-AI role (GRAIN_DUAL_PURPOSE)

pros.claim: Treating banding as structural puts countermeasures in the pipeline by default instead of reacting post-upload
pros.example: a standing high-bit-depth grade project plus a subtle grain node so every export ships pre-defended gradients

cons.claim: Deband filtering and grain both soften or texture areas that the luxury aesthetic wants pristine
cons.example: a deband pass smearing the fine edge of a marble vein while smoothing the wall gradient behind it

failure_modes: grading in 8-bit end to end and baking banding into the master
leaving large smooth gradients undithered and letting the platform re-encode band them
acceptance_tests: the analysis states the 8-bit/4:2:0 structural mechanics and applies all three countermeasures (high bit depth, ~1-2% dither/grain, deband on affected regions)
revisit_triggers: a test upload still shows banding despite countermeasures

base.update_signal: post-upload banding despite defenses or a platform encoder change alters the countermeasure set

nodes.definition: Protect shadow detail from the encoder. Do not grade intentional shadow detail right at black: heavy encoders crush near-black macroblocks FIRST, so detail meant to survive must sit a few code values above 0; and the graded reel must be checked ON A PHONE after an ACTUAL test upload, not just in the NLE, because the crush only exists after the platform re-encode [ESTIMATE - colorist craft plus codec behavior, medium-high confidence per grounding file]. This node disciplines the look's shadow side: the luxury grade's 'lifted-but-not-milky blacks' is not only an aesthetic move — the lift is also the compression-survival margin. The phone check is the only ground truth; an NLE-only sign-off on shadow detail is a guess about what Instagram's encoder will do to it.

included: keeping intentional shadow detail a few code values above 0
the phone-after-test-upload verification as ground truth
the lifted-blacks lift as compression margin
excluded: the full encode settings (DELIVERY_ENCODE_SETTINGS)
publishing workflow around the test upload (media-manager file)

pros.claim: A few code values of black headroom cheaply insures the moody shadow detail the luxury look depends on
pros.example: a dim wine-cellar clip keeping its bottle-row texture after re-encode because the detail sat above the crush zone

cons.claim: The phone-check loop adds a test-upload round trip to every reel sign-off

acceptance_tests: the analysis keeps intentional shadow detail a few code values above 0 and verifies the graded reel on a phone after an actual test upload before sign-off
revisit_triggers: a phone check reveals crush despite the headroom, meaning the margin is too small

base.update_signal: phone-check failures or encoder behavior changes resize the black headroom

nodes.definition: Ship the graded master in the compression-safest way the research supports. Instagram re-encodes all uploads; practitioner guidance: deliver 1080-wide (upscaling beyond gives no benefit and raises compression risk), ~3,500-5,000 kbps cited for Reels-length content, Rec.709/SDR delivery, enable 'Upload at highest quality', and upload from the app rather than through third-party re-encoders [FACT/excerpt - compression-fix guide, source 32; the exact bitrate window is third-party advice, NOT Meta-published — held as ESTIMATE, medium confidence]. The realistic tool path per the grounding file: assemble/beat-lock mobile or desktop, grade and match in Resolve, export the master, upload from the IG app with highest quality on [ESTIMATE - tooling landscape, medium confidence]. No Meta-published encoder spec is claimed anywhere — the numbers stay tagged as third-party.

the hybrid assemble-grade-export-upload tool path
excluded: posting cadence, captions and analytics (media-manager file)

nodes.definition: Use one knob for two goals. Subtle film grain simultaneously (a) fights banding by breaking up smooth gradient areas — a countermeasure with citable debanding basis — and (b) reads as a 'shot on film, not AI' cue, serving the owner's #1 must-not-look-AI requirement at the same time as delivery QC [FACT/excerpt on grain/dither as a banding countermeasure - sources 33-34; the anti-AI alignment is ESTIMATE - inference, medium-high confidence per grounding file]. The bound: very heavy grain WASTES BITRATE and can smear under re-encode — the encoder spends bits on the noise and the platform's second encode mushes it — so the dose stays subtle (the ~1-2% fine-grain range cited for debanding is the working default). Grain is therefore dosed once, at the master level, as part of the house look's texture, not added ad hoc per clip.

pros.example: a 1-2% fine grain layer that both holds the villa-wall gradient through re-encode and removes the too-clean digital sheen AI clips carry

nodes.definition: Operate the grade layer's starred rubric row in the director feedback loop. Every generated still/clip frame is scored on exposure before entering the timeline: skin at the correct level on the WAVEFORM; highlights ROLLED, not clipped; blacks NOT crushed [FACT/excerpt on the scopes practice - source 28; the rubric weighting is ESTIMATE - designed in the grounding file, to be calibrated against real batches]. Exposure is one of the STARRED rows: a zero score = automatic regenerate, because clipped or crushed data is an irrecoverable-in-post failure — no grade can synthesize tonal information the generation never delivered [ESTIMATE - triage design, high confidence]. This gate is where grading exerts power over generation: rejecting unusable exposure at the still stage is cheaper than any downstream rescue attempt.

conflict_axes.description: The teal-orange mechanism rewards intensity with measurable pop, while the classic-luxurious brief demands muted highlights, low chroma and a whisper of teal at most.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: restraint wins on the global grade; recover separation via hue-of-skin-vs-field, tonal contrast and depth of field instead of saturation

conflict_axes.name: global LUT efficiency vs per-clip correction
conflict_axes.description: One baked LUT promises one-click consistency, but LUTs are dumb transforms that amplify per-clip mismatch when used as a substitute for balancing.
poles: apply the house LUT everywhere immediately
balance every clip to the hero first
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: balance-first always; the LUT sits last in the chain on top of matched clips and is never bent per clip

conflict_axes.name: filmic shadow mood vs compression survival
conflict_axes.description: The luxury look wants deep, moody shadow rendering, but heavy encoders crush near-black macroblocks first, destroying detail graded at black.
poles: shadow detail a few code values above 0
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep intentional shadow detail above the crush zone — the lifted-but-not-milky black is both the aesthetic and the survival margin — and verify on a phone after a test upload

conflict_axes.name: grain texture vs bitrate budget
conflict_axes.description: Grain fights banding and reads filmic, but the encoder spends bits on noise: heavy grain wastes bitrate and smears under the platform's re-encode.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hold the ~1-2% fine-grain range and let phone checks after test uploads arbitrate the dose

conflict_axes.name: automated match speed vs eye-plus-scopes accuracy
conflict_axes.description: Automated shot-match handles volume across many 3-6 s clips, but the professional practice holds it is a starting point only, always refined by eye and scopes.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: auto-match starts, waveform/parade/vectorscope finish; a clip is matched when the scopes say so, not when the button was pressed

conflict_axes.name: per-model prior vs per-clip reality
conflict_axes.description: Learned per-model trim presets speed up matching but may encode small-batch noise or go stale after a model update, misleading the very step they serve.
poles: measure each clip fresh against the hero
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: preset as prior, hero match as authority; retire and relearn any preset that increases the residual

conflict_axes.name: fix-in-post vs regenerate
conflict_axes.description: Grading can rescue moderate mismatch, but clipped highlights, crushed blacks and mid-clip drift are irrecoverable or costlier to fight in post than to regenerate at the still stage, the cheap place to fail.
poles: rescue the clip in the grade
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: starred exposure failures and matched-pair failures regenerate; only in-gamut, boundary-stable clips are worth grading effort

conflict_axes.name: core-grade coherence vs fitness-accent differentiation
conflict_axes.description: Fitness posts want extra contrast/saturation energy, but the grid's coherence — one house grade across all covers and posts — is what carries the luxury positioning.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: allow a bounded trim within the same palette family; the profile grid is the test, and posts that read as a different account lose the accent

edge_cases.description: The two personas' skin lands at visibly different vectorscope positions after the look is applied, breaking character consistency at the grade layer
edge_cases.trigger: different generation batches render the two personas' skin with different undertones
edge_cases.mitigation: key each persona's skin back to the single saved per-persona target on the vectorscope skin line before sign-off; if the gap exceeds what a key can close naturally, regenerate the worse clip

edge_cases.description: A clip arrives from a model with no learned trim preset yet (new model or first session), so no pre-correction exists
edge_cases.trigger: onboarding a new AI video model into the pipeline
edge_cases.mitigation: match the clip to the hero fully manually, record the applied correction, and seed the model's trim preset from the first few such measurements — never guess a signature

edge_cases.description: A clip matches the hero at its first frame but drifts warm/teal mid-clip, so any static correction is wrong for part of the clip
edge_cases.trigger: intra-clip temporal drift in the generated footage
edge_cases.mitigation: trim to the stable segment first, regenerate second, keyframed correction only as a last resort; re-run boundary QC after any trim because the cut frames changed

edge_cases.description: The best-skin candidate for hero has clipped highlights, so declaring it would propagate an irrecoverable flaw to the whole reel
edge_cases.trigger: hero selection where no clip is strong on both skin and exposure
edge_cases.mitigation: the exposure gate disqualifies the clipped candidate; declare the best clip that passes no-clip/no-crush, or regenerate a hero-grade clip before matching anything

edge_cases.description: A cut boundary passes the luminance window but a hue mismatch still reads at the cut
edge_cases.trigger: QC tuned on luminance only, or a hue shift too small for the window but visible in motion
edge_cases.mitigation: the window is luminance AND hue; check the parade/vectorscope at both boundary frames and re-match the offending clip rather than nudging one frame

edge_cases.description: Banding appears only after Instagram's re-encode while the NLE preview and exported master both look clean
edge_cases.trigger: the platform's 8-bit 4:2:0 re-encode of smooth luxury gradients
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the phone-after-test-upload check as the only ground truth; raise the fine-grain/dither dose or deband the affected region and re-test upload

edge_cases.description: The house LUT is applied to an unbalanced clip as a shortcut and the mismatch gets amplified into the styled image
edge_cases.trigger: time pressure tempting a LUT-only grade of a fresh batch
edge_cases.mitigation: hard rule: no LUT on unbalanced clips; if the deadline cannot fit balancing, cut the reel with fewer, balanced clips instead

edge_cases.description: Successive fitness-accent posts each nudge saturation a little further until the grid visibly splits into two looks
edge_cases.trigger: accent creep across posts with no grid-level check
edge_cases.mitigation: fix the accent as one saved trim (not a per-post adjustment) and review the profile grid as a whole before each publish; posts breaking palette-family coherence lose the accent

edge_cases.description: A designed start/end frame pair matches perfectly as stills but the generated video wanders in color between the boundaries
edge_cases.trigger: end-frame conditioning controlling the boundary, not the path
edge_cases.mitigation: keep clips 3-5 s with simple consistent lighting prompts, and run drift triage plus boundary QC on the generated clip anyway — a matched pair never exempts the clip

edge_cases.description: Shadow detail graded right at code value 0 survives the NLE and the master but is crushed to nothing by the platform encoder
edge_cases.trigger: grading moody shadow detail without near-black headroom
edge_cases.mitigation: keep intentional shadow detail a few code values above 0 (the lifted-black margin) and verify on a phone after an actual test upload before publishing

edge_cases.description: An AI clip's actual delivery characteristics (color space, bit depth, fps) contradict the display-referred Rec.709-ish assumption, and the exact specs remain undocumented
edge_cases.trigger: a generation batch behaving unexpectedly under the standard normalization; the blocker is named — exact Higgsfield delivery specs are [UNKNOWN here], owned by the MCP-surface research file
edge_cases.mitigation: stop bulk grading, characterize the batch on scopes, record the observed behavior, and escalate the spec question to the MCP-surface file rather than inventing a delivery spec

workflow.action: Set up the working space and timeline color management for display-referred Rec.709-ish sources
workflow.description: Normalize all clips into one working space under the assumption AI clips arrive display-referred, flagging the assumption as revisable when actual Higgsfield delivery specs arrive
workflow.artifact: a project/timeline color-management setting with the Rec.709-ish assumption noted
workflow.gate: all clips load into one working space with no double transform (no log-conversion LUT applied to display-referred files)

workflow.action: Gate incoming frames on the starred exposure row
workflow.description: Score every candidate still/clip frame: skin at correct waveform level, highlights rolled not clipped, blacks not crushed; a zero auto-regenerates
workflow.artifact: a pass/fail exposure score per incoming frame with regenerate orders for zeros
workflow.gate: no clipped-highlight or crushed-black frame enters the timeline

workflow.action: Grade the designed start/end frame pairs before video generation
workflow.description: Hold every clip-boundary still pair to the same house grade target, same skin values and a narrow luminance window; regenerate failing stills at the cheap stage
workflow.artifact: approved frame-pair set per reel cleared for video generation
workflow.gate: every pair sits inside the grade/skin/luminance window on both frames

workflow.action: Declare the hero clip for the reel
workflow.description: Pick the one clip with best skin plus best exposure that itself passes the no-clip/no-crush gate; its balanced state becomes the match target
workflow.artifact: a named hero clip per reel with its scope reads recorded
workflow.gate: the hero passes the exposure gate and carries the persona skin target

workflow.action: Apply per-model trim presets to all non-hero clips
workflow.description: Pre-correct each clip with its model's learned offset/temp/sat trim (if one exists) so hero matching starts from a smaller gap; new models get no guessed preset
workflow.artifact: trimmed clips plus an updated per-model preset log
workflow.gate: each applied preset demonstrably reduces the clip-to-hero residual; presets that do not are retired

workflow.action: Match every clip to the hero on the scopes
workflow.description: Per clip: luminance on the waveform, then white balance on the RGB parade, then skin on the vectorscope; auto shot-match as a start only, refined by eye plus scopes
workflow.artifact: per-clip balance corrections under the (not yet applied) house LUT
workflow.gate: each clip's waveform/parade/vectorscope reads sit within the match window of the hero

workflow.action: Group clips by scene/location/batch and propagate shared corrections
workflow.description: Organize matched clips into groups mapped to locations and generation batches so shared casts are corrected once at group level with small per-clip trims
workflow.artifact: a grouped timeline with group-level correction nodes
workflow.gate: no identical correction is duplicated across clips of one group; no clip sits in a group whose cast it does not share

workflow.description: Qualify/mask skin before the creative look or key it back after, landing both personas on the single saved skin target across every clip
workflow.artifact: skin qualifiers/keys per clip with both personas on the shared vectorscope target
workflow.gate: no gray or cyan-tinged skin anywhere; both personas' skin reads match the saved target

workflow.action: Apply the house creative LUT globally
workflow.description: Place the one baked warm-neutral luxury LUT last in the chain on top of all balanced, skin-protected clips (fitness posts add their bounded trim above it)
workflow.artifact: the fully looked timeline sharing one house transform
workflow.gate: the LUT sits only on balanced clips and is identical across all clips, covers and posts

workflow.description: Step through every cut; the two frames either side of each boundary must sit within the tight luminance/hue window; failures route back to hero matching
workflow.artifact: a boundary QC checklist with per-cut pass/fail
workflow.gate: every cut boundary passes the window; zero boundary-local hacks

workflow.action: Apply banding and black-crush defenses to the master
workflow.description: Keep the grade in high bit depth to the end, add the ~1-2% fine grain/dither dose at master level, deband affected gradient regions, and confirm shadow detail sits above the crush zone
workflow.gate: no visible banding or crushed intentional shadow detail in the high-bit-depth master

workflow.action: Export, test-upload and verify on a phone
workflow.description: Export 1080-wide Rec.709/SDR within the third-party bitrate window, upload from the IG app with highest quality on, and check banding/blacks/skin on a phone after the actual re-encode
workflow.gate: the phone check after a real test upload shows no banding, no crushed blacks, and skin on target

dominance_rules.rule: When look strength and skin fidelity conflict, skin fidelity wins
dominance_rules.rationale: gray or cyan-tinged skin is an instant AI/cheap-filter tell that violates the owner's #1 must-not-look-AI requirement; no separation gain is worth it
dominance_rules.trigger: any teal push, desaturation or look intensity change that would land on faces
dominance_rules.action: qualify skin out of the look or key it back to the saved per-persona target before sign-off

dominance_rules.rule: When LUT convenience and per-clip balance conflict, per-clip balance wins
dominance_rules.rationale: LUTs are dumb transforms that amplify mismatch on unbalanced clips; a styled mismatch is worse than an unstyled one
dominance_rules.trigger: temptation to apply the house LUT to a fresh unbalanced batch
dominance_rules.action: balance every clip to the hero first; if time is short, ship fewer balanced clips rather than more unbalanced ones

dominance_rules.rule: When post-rescue and regeneration conflict on a starred failure, regeneration wins
dominance_rules.rationale: clipped highlights, crushed blacks and broken frames are irrecoverable in post — no grade synthesizes tonal data the generation never delivered — and stills are the cheap place to fail
dominance_rules.trigger: a zero on the starred exposure row or a failed start/end frame pair
dominance_rules.action: reject and regenerate at the still stage; do not enter the timeline or spend grading effort on the frame

dominance_rules.rule: When the NLE preview and the phone-after-upload check disagree, the phone wins
dominance_rules.rationale: banding and black crush are produced by the platform re-encode, which only the post-upload phone check observes
dominance_rules.trigger: any disagreement between the master's look in the NLE and the test upload on a phone
dominance_rules.action: recalibrate grain/deband/black headroom against the phone result and re-export; never sign off on NLE preview alone

dominance_rules.rule: When automated shot-match and eye-plus-scopes refinement disagree, scopes win
dominance_rules.rationale: the professional practice holds auto-match is a starting point only; scope reads are the objective match evidence
dominance_rules.trigger: auto-match output that looks acceptable but sits outside the waveform/parade/vectorscope window
dominance_rules.action: refine manually until the scope reads sit within the hero window

dominance_rules.rule: When a per-model trim preset and the hero match disagree, the hero match wins
dominance_rules.rationale: presets are priors learned from small batches and can encode noise or go stale after model updates; the per-clip match is the measurement
dominance_rules.trigger: a preset-corrected clip still off the hero window, or a preset that increases the residual
dominance_rules.action: finish the match manually, then retire and relearn the preset from fresh measurements

dominance_rules.rule: When fitness-post punch and grid coherence conflict, grid coherence wins
dominance_rules.rationale: one house grade across the grid carries the classic-luxurious positioning harder than any single post's energy
dominance_rules.trigger: a fitness-accent trim that makes the post read outside the palette family on the grid
dominance_rules.action: pull the accent back inside the family or drop it for that post

dominance_rules.rule: When memory and the research file's honesty tag disagree, the tag wins
dominance_rules.rationale: this KB's authority is the grounding file; model signatures, delivery specs and platform numbers it marked [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] must not be silently upgraded to fact
dominance_rules.trigger: any temptation to state a Higgsfield delivery spec, per-model signature or Meta encoder number not carried by the research
dominance_rules.action: carry the [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] tag forward, name the owning research file, and measure instead of asserting

anti_rework_rules.rule: Balance every clip to the hero BEFORE applying the house LUT
anti_rework_rules.prevents: regrading the whole reel after the LUT amplifies per-clip mismatch into the styled image

anti_rework_rules.rule: Declare and exposure-gate the hero BEFORE matching any clip
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-matching every clip in the reel when a late-discovered hero flaw (clipped highlights, biased skin) forces re-declaration

anti_rework_rules.rule: Grade and approve start/end frame pairs BEFORE spending video-generation credits
anti_rework_rules.prevents: paying for video generations whose boundaries were doomed at the still stage — the expensive place to fail

anti_rework_rules.rule: Lock the shared per-persona skin targets BEFORE grading the first reel
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-keying skin across every published post when the two personas' targets are found inconsistent later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Learn a model's trim preset from its FIRST batches before bulk generation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: hand-correcting the same systematic per-model cast on dozens of clips that one measured preset would have pre-corrected

anti_rework_rules.rule: Keep the grade in high bit depth until the final export
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a full re-grade when banding baked into an 8-bit intermediate surfaces at delivery

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run the cut-boundary QC pass BEFORE export
anti_rework_rules.prevents: export/upload/phone-check cycles burned on boundary mismatches that a timeline pass would have caught

anti_rework_rules.rule: Do a test upload with a phone check BEFORE the publish schedule depends on the reel
anti_rework_rules.prevents: pulling and re-delivering a published post after the platform re-encode reveals banding or crushed blacks

iteration_protocol.trigger: a cut boundary fails the luminance/hue window at QC
iteration_protocol.action: route the offending clip back through the hero match (waveform, parade, vectorscope) and re-run the boundary pass; never patch the boundary locally

iteration_protocol.trigger: either persona's skin drifts off the saved vectorscope target in any clip or post
iteration_protocol.action: re-key skin toward the shared target; if the key cannot close the gap naturally, regenerate the clip — and audit neighboring clips from the same batch

iteration_protocol.trigger: the phone check after a test upload shows banding or crushed blacks the NLE never showed
iteration_protocol.action: raise the fine-grain/dither dose or deband the region, re-check the near-black headroom, re-export and re-test-upload until the phone passes

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new AI video model is onboarded or an existing model ships a version update
iteration_protocol.action: grade its first batch fully manually against the hero, measure the systematic offset, and seed/relearn that model's trim preset from the measurements

iteration_protocol.trigger: the MCP-surface file documents actual Higgsfield delivery specs (color space, bit depth, fps)
iteration_protocol.action: replace the display-referred Rec.709-ish assumption with the documented specs, revalidate the working-space setup, and re-check whether any technical LUT belongs in the chain

iteration_protocol.trigger: intra-clip drift is found in a clip already on the timeline
iteration_protocol.action: trim to the stable segment first, regenerate second, keyframe only as last resort; then re-run boundary QC because the cut frames changed

iteration_protocol.trigger: the house look is revised (palette shift, rolloff change, grain texture change)
iteration_protocol.action: rebake the single house LUT, reapply it across the timeline, re-run boundary QC, and review the profile grid so old covers and new posts still cohere

priority_rationale: Concept and instrument nodes (log/Rec.709, chain order, scopes, the AI-delivery reframe) come first because every look, matching and delivery decision is expressed in their vocabulary; the look family (mechanism, luxury translation, skin, LUT) precedes matching because the hero and the match window are defined against an approved look and skin target; matching precedes delivery because banding, crush and encode defenses operate on an already-matched, looked master.
